lead: At fixed temperature the equilibrium constant of a gas reaction is fixed. Pressure and inert gas change the mole fractions inside that constant without changing the constant itself. For an ideal gas K = K<sub>y</sub> (P/P°)<sup>Σν</sup>, so the sign of Σν tells which way the mixture moves. Industry uses the rule directly: ammonia synthesis runs at high pressure because it makes fewer moles, while cracking and dehydrogenation run at low pressure or with steam dilution because they make more moles.
prereq: You need: equilibrium constants and composition from 7.5, and equilibrium conversion from 7.6.

sections.h3: Pressure changes the split, not K

blocks.text: At fixed temperature, K for a gas reaction does not change when pressure changes. What changes is the way K is split between mole fractions and pressure. For an ideal gas, the activity of species i is a<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub> P/P°, where y<sub>i</sub> is mole fraction, P is total pressure, and P° is standard pressure, 1 bar.

blocks.where: a<sub>i</sub> is activity, y<sub>i</sub> is mole fraction, P is total pressure, P° is standard pressure (1 bar), ν<sub>i</sub> is stoichiometric coefficient (positive for products, negative for reactants), Σν = Σν<sub>i</sub>, and K<sub>y</sub> = ∏ y<sub>i</sub><sup>ν<sub>i</sub></sup>.

blocks.text: At fixed T, K is fixed. Rearranging gives K<sub>y</sub> = K (P/P°)<sup>−Σν</sup>. If Σν > 0, raising P lowers the K<sub>y</sub> that K requires at the new pressure, so the mixture moves toward reactants until it reaches that new, lower K<sub>y</sub>. If Σν < 0, raising P favours products. If Σν = 0, pressure cancels and there is no ideal-gas shift.

sections.h3: Inert gas dilutes the reacting mixture

blocks.text: An inert gas does not appear in the reaction stoichiometry. It still occupies volume and adds to total moles. For an ideal gas at total pressure P, the partial pressure of i is p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub> P = n<sub>i</sub> P / n<sub>total</sub>. Adding inert raises n<sub>total</sub>. At fixed T and P, p<sub>i</sub> of every reactant and product falls.

This is dilution. It acts like lowering total pressure while keeping the same mole numbers of reactants and products. The equilibrium shifts toward the side with more moles. So inerts raise conversion when Σν > 0 and lower conversion when Σν < 0. When Σν = 0, inerts have no ideal-gas effect on composition. At fixed T and V the case is different: adding inert does not change p<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub> RT/V for the reacting species, so for an ideal gas the composition does not shift at all; only the total pressure rises.

At fixed T, changing volume changes the pressure of a gas by P = nRT/V. Halving V roughly doubles P. The composition shift follows the same Σν rule: compression acts like higher pressure. For a reaction that makes more moles, compression lowers conversion; for one that makes fewer moles, compression raises conversion.

For liquid-phase reactions, pressure has little effect on K and activity coefficients over ordinary pressures. The pressure effect becomes noticeable near the critical point or at very high pressures, where fugacity coefficients differ from unity. Then replace ideal-gas activities by ai = yi φi P/P°, with φi the fugacity coefficient. This is the link to nonideal gas treatment in 7.8.

examples.question: For A ⇌ 2B, K = 0.222 at 400 K. A feed of 1 mol A is at 400 K. (a) Find X<sub>A</sub> at P = 1 bar, 0.5 bar and 2 bar. (b) Find X<sub>A</sub> at 1 bar if 1 mol inert is also fed.
steps: Let ξ be the extent in mol. With 1 mol A initially and no inert: n<sub>A</sub> = 1 − ξ, n<sub>B</sub> = 2ξ, n<sub>total</sub> = 1 + ξ. Conversion of A is X<sub>A</sub> = ξ/1 = ξ.
Mole fractions are y<sub>A</sub> = (1 − ξ)/(1 + ξ) and y<sub>B</sub> = 2ξ/(1 + ξ). For A ⇌ 2B, Σν = 2 − 1 = 1. With P° = 1 bar, K = (P/P°) × 4ξ²/(1 − ξ²).

With 1 mol inert at 1 bar: n<sub>total</sub> = 2 + ξ, y<sub>A</sub> = (1 − ξ)/(2 + ξ), y<sub>B</sub> = 2ξ/(2 + ξ). K = 4ξ²/[(2 + ξ)(1 − ξ)]. Substituting K = 0.222 gives 0.222(2 − ξ − ξ²) = 4ξ², which rearranges to 4.222ξ² + 0.222ξ − 0.444 = 0.
examples.answer: At 0.5 bar X<sub>A</sub> = 0.316; at 1 bar X<sub>A</sub> = 0.229; at 2 bar X<sub>A</sub> = 0.164; with 1 mol inert at 1 bar X<sub>A</sub> = 0.299.
examples.check:
import math
K = 0.222

def x_extent(P, inert=0.0):
    a = 4.0 * P + K
    b = K * inert
    c = -K * (1.0 + inert)
    disc = b * b - 4.0 * a * c
    return (-b + math.sqrt(disc)) / (2.0 * a)

print(f"{x_extent(0.5):.3f}")
print(f"{x_extent(1.0):.3f}")
print(f"{x_extent(2.0):.3f}")
print(f"{x_extent(1.0, 1.0):.3f}")

examples.question: Ammonia synthesis, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, has K = 0.100 at 500 K. A stoichiometric feed (1 mol N₂, 3 mol H₂) reaches equilibrium as an ideal gas. Find the conversion of N₂ at 1 bar and at 100 bar, and at 100 bar when the feed also carries 0.444 mol argon (10 mol % of the feed).
steps: Moles: n<sub>N₂</sub> = 1 − ξ, n<sub>H₂</sub> = 3(1 − ξ), n<sub>NH₃</sub> = 2ξ, n<sub>T</sub> = 4 − 2ξ; Σν = −2. Then K = [y<sub>NH₃</sub>²/(y<sub>N₂</sub> y<sub>H₂</sub>³)](P/P°)<sup>−2</sup> = 16ξ²(2 − ξ)²/[27(1 − ξ)⁴] × (P°/P)².
At 100 bar the same left side must equal 0.100 × 100² = 1000. Trial ξ = 0.84 gives 859 and ξ = 0.85 gives 1118, so ξ = 0.846: X = 84.6 %, y<sub>NH₃</sub> = 1.692/2.308 = 0.733.
With 0.444 mol argon at 100 bar, n<sub>T</sub> = 4.444 − 2ξ, so the factor (4 − 2ξ)² becomes (4.444 − 2ξ)². Solving gives ξ = 0.832: X = 83.2 % and y<sub>NH₃</sub> = 0.599.
K is 0.100 in every case; only the split between the mole fractions and (P/P°)<sup>−2</sup> changes.
examples.answer: Raising the pressure from 1 to 100 bar lifts the N₂ conversion from 15.8 % to 84.6 % because Σν = −2; 10 mol % argon in the feed at 100 bar lowers it to 83.2 %.

traps: Saying pressure changes K. At fixed T, K is fixed; pressure changes activities and K<sub>y</sub>.
Reversing the Σν rule. For A ⇌ 2B, Σν = +1, so higher pressure lowers conversion.
Putting inerts into the K expression. Inerts do not appear in K; they change n<sub>total</sub> and hence mole fractions.
Confusing fixed P with fixed V when inert is added. At fixed P the inert dilutes reactants; at fixed V it does not change their partial pressures in an ideal gas.

quiz.q: Define Σν for a gas reaction and give its value for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
quiz.a: Σν is the sum of stoichiometric coefficients, positive for products and negative for reactants. For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, Σν = 2 − (1 + 3) = −2.

quiz.q: Why does high pressure favour ammonia synthesis?
quiz.a: The reaction has Σν = −2, so K<sub>y</sub> = K(P/P°)². Raising P increases K<sub>y</sub>, which means the equilibrium mixture must move toward products, the side with fewer moles. K itself does not change at fixed T.

quiz.q: For A ⇌ 2B, K = 0.222 at 400 K. Feed 1 mol A. Find the pressure that gives X<sub>A</sub> = 0.10.
A gas reaction has Σν = 0. The feed contains 30% inert at fixed T and P. Does the inert change equilibrium conversion? Explain using K<sub>y</sub>.
quiz.a: No ideal-gas effect. K = K<sub>y</sub>(P/P°)<sup>0</sup> = K<sub>y</sub>. Since Σν = 0, K<sub>y</sub> = ∏y<sub>i</sub><sup>ν<sub>i</sub></sup> = ∏n<sub>i</sub><sup>ν<sub>i</sub></sup>, so n<sub>total</sub> cancels. The inert changes n<sub>total</sub> but not the equilibrium relation.

quiz.q: For A ⇌ 2B, K = 0.222 at 400 K. Feed 1 mol A and 1 mol inert at P = 2 bar. Find X<sub>A</sub>.
quiz.a: n<sub>A</sub> = 1 − ξ, n<sub>B</sub> = 2ξ, n<sub>total</sub> = 2 + ξ. K = 2 × 4ξ²/[(2 + ξ)(1 − ξ)] = 8ξ²/[(2 + ξ)(1 − ξ)]. This gives 8.222ξ² + 0.222ξ − 0.444 = 0, so ξ = 0.219 and X<sub>A</sub> = 0.219.

quiz.q: At fixed T, a reaction with Σν > 0 is run at fixed V. You add inert gas. Does conversion change in an ideal gas? Compare with fixed P.
quiz.a: At fixed V, p<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>RT/V, so adding inert does not change the partial pressures of reactants and products. There is no dilution and no shift. At fixed P, adding inert raises n<sub>total</sub>, lowers p<sub>i</sub>, and shifts the equilibrium toward more moles, so conversion rises when Σν > 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. In high-pressure gas systems, fugacity coefficients replace ideal-gas activities, so the pressure lever acts through both P and φ<sub>i</sub>. Search next for 'fugacity coefficient high pressure equilibrium'.
